transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Riley Zhang (Redwood AE), Jordan Kim (Redwood SE), Alex Soto (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Horizon CTO), Liam O'Connor (Platform Eng), Emily Ruiz (SRE), Marcus Lee (Data Eng)

Auto-summary (auto): quick demo of long-history behavior, backpressure and timeouts, and ops playbook link shared

[00:00] Riley Zhang: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we should be green to start, uh, Riley from Redwood here, joined by Jordan and Alex on the SE side. How's it going Priya?
[00:17] Priya Nair: Good, thanks. We have about 45 minutes, we wanted to see the long-session behavior especially when we push high TPS and we get intermittent network blips — our engineering team calls it connection flutter.
[00:32] Jordan Kim: Great, that's exactly what we'll walk through. Quick agenda: API/Console demo, Optimize suggestions (batching/quant), then a short run of a synthetic load and a health/ops playbook for incident response.
[00:50] Liam O'Connor: Quick question on scope — we plan to run up to 50k requests per second in some windows, does that align with the Dedicated capacity versus Hosted?
[01:05] Riley Zhang: Yes, we can cover both. For consistent 50k TPS we'd recommend Dedicated capacity or a reserved burst plan; Hosted can handle spikes but you'd want dedicated pools for predictable latency SLOs.
[01:20] Emily Ruiz: Also, are we able to keep a 1M token rolling context per session? Our agents keep very long histories and truncation is a pain.
[01:32] Alex Soto: So we typically advise a combo: rolling KV-cache with pinned prefixes for the last N tokens plus a TTL for old context, and you can offload cold history to embeddings for retrieval. In the Console you'll see KV-cache settings, eviction thresholds, and prefix pinning.
[01:50] Marcus Lee: When you say KV-cache, sometimes the docs show K-V cash in the transcripts — just making sure it's the same cache you referenced.
[01:58] Jordan Kim: (laughs) yes, same thing, kv-cache — apologies for the auto-transcript.
[02:06] Riley Zhang: I'll share the deck and the ops playbook after the call. Link: https://redwood.demo/playbooks/long-history-ops (note: internal link)

--- API demo / streaming playground ---

[02:40] Jordan Kim: Alright, switching to the API. I'm going to show two flows side-by-side: one using streaming responses with a long context pinned in the kv cache and one with chunked, non-streaming calls.
[03:00] Jordan Kim: Here you can see the request: model, max_tokens, stream=true, session_id, and we attach a cache_key with the pinned prefix. The Console also shows realtime telemetry — per-token latency and per-session token counts.
[03:23] Liam O'Connor: What happens when you have many concurrent sessions each with huge histories — do you evict aggressively? What's the eviction policy?
[03:36] Alex Soto: Eviction is LRU-ish, but we have hot-key protection plus a grace window so if a session is actively streaming it won't evict mid-response. You can adjust the grace window in the Console — default is 60s.
[03:52] Emily Ruiz: If we see a node restart and long sessions reconnect, do we get partial history loss?
[03:59] Jordan Kim: For Hosted we keep replication and automatic fallback; for Dedicated you can enable persistent NVM-backed cache to avoid cold starts, or use our offload to object store. Note that long context persistence increases cost footprint.

--- Synthetic high-TPS run (demo) ---

[04:30] Riley Zhang: We'll kick off a short synthetic with bursty traffic and simulated network blips to show streaming backpressure behaviour. We'll instrument logging so you can see the per-request route-level fallback, and the console will surface drop rates and backpressure events.
[04:49] Jordan Kim: Starting the synthetic now — config: 20k sustained, 40k bursts, 1000 concurrent sessions, long-history per session (~250k tokens), streaming true, grace window 60s.
[05:08] (background instrumentation noise)
[05:15] Marcus Lee: Heads up, our real workload will be more like 50k with varying session lengths — consider this a baseline.
[05:23] Jordan Kim: Understood. Starting simulated jitter now.
[05:40] [05:40] System: first burst initiated — console shows CPU and GPU utilization climbing on the Dedicated pool.
[05:55] Emily Ruiz: I'm seeing increased tail latency in the telemetry, is that expected?
[06:02] Jordan Kim: Yes at the burst peak the system prioritizes median latency via autoscaling, but if the queue fills you get backpressure signals. Note the streaming client sees partial chunks and has built-in reconnection strategies — we'll show the reconnection handshake in the logs.
[06:23] Riley Zhang: Also note the smart routing — some requests are routed to a cheaper model variant with quantization when latency slack is acceptable; we surface that in the trace as fallback_variant:.
[06:45] Priya Nair: We're concerned about quality regressions when falling back — how do we measure/regressions?
[06:52] Alex Soto: Great question. Optimize ties regressions to eval sets and we've per-route quality thresholds. If a fallback causes eval drift above threshold, we block automatic fallback and alert. You can tune those thresholds per route.

--- Demonstrated backpressure behaviors ---

[07:20] Jordan Kim: Now I'm going to force a connection flutter — simulate repeated short disconnects for a subset of sessions. You'll see streaming clients get an EPIPE-like reconnection, the server will hold KV cache for the grace window, and if the session reconnects within the window we replay the KV context without re-fetching from object store.
[07:45] Liam O'Connor: Ok and what's the TTL for that grace window? Can we make it longer than 60s?
[07:51] Jordan Kim: Yes, in Dedicated you can set it up to several hours depending on memory considerations. Console exposes this as 'grace_window_ms' slider.
[08:05] Emily Ruiz: If a reconnection occurs after eviction, does the client get a partial state or an error?
[08:12] Jordan Kim: They get a fallback policy response — either a truncated history or we reroute to a cold-start flow that fetches embeddings for context, dependent on your fallback policy. We showed logs where fallback_reason=eviction in the trace.

[08:35] Riley Zhang: I'm going to open the Console to show the fallback dashboard — you can filter by fallback_reason, by session, and by route. Link to recording will be included.

--- Security and compliance discussion ---

[09:00] Priya Nair: Security is critical — we're in regulated finance. We need SOC 2 type II, SAML SSO, HSM/KMS for key management, and audit logs retained for 7 years. Can Redwood support that in Dedicated or Private?
[09:20] Riley Zhang: Yes. Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations, SAML SSO, RBAC. Private on-prem adds the air-gapped option for full data residency. For audit logs 7 years is high but we can do extended retention via log export to your object store — that will be an add-on. We'll share SOC2 attestation and the compliance pack.
[09:40] Marcus Lee: Any gotchas around PII in training telemetry? We need strict no-training SLA.
[09:45] Alex Soto: We have no-training agreements and can disable telemetry ingestion for models used with PII; also you can use redwood private with a local-only control plane. We'll attach the legal addendum.

--- Incident playbook / console alerts ---

[10:10] Jordan Kim: Walkthrough of the incident flow: if you see streaming chunk drop > 0.5% we trigger an alert, we can automatically fall back routes to a stable variant, scale up Dedicated pools, and notify on-call. Console has a 'playbook' button that triggers the runbook.
[10:30] Emily Ruiz: Can that be automated with our PagerDuty?
[10:33] Jordan Kim: Yes, PD integration is standard.

--- Deep dive: timeout modes and chunk reassembly ---

[11:00] Jordan Kim: There are three timeout modes: immediate-fail, graceful-wait (maintain KV context until grace window), and stream-shed (drop streaming chunks older than X). For your workload with many short blips, I'd suggest graceful-wait with a longer grace window plus higher backpressure thresholds.
[11:25] Priya Nair: What's the CPU/GPU tradeoff there? If we keep long kv-cache per session memory usage goes up — where do costs escalate?
[11:33] Alex Soto: Memory and GPU memory increases are the main costs. Optimize will recommend quantization and batching profiles to reduce footprint; we can run profiling to show cost delta between 16-bit and 8-bit quant configs.

[11:50] Marcus Lee: Are there any known pathologies where streaming reconnection leads to duplicated outputs? We've seen that in some libraries.
[11:58] Jordan Kim: We handle idempotency tokens at the request layer; if you use the session_id + message_id the server dedups replays. But if clients retry incorrectly, you can get duplicates — we'll show the dedup logs.

--- Walkthrough of Console Optimize suggestions ---

[12:30] Jordan Kim: In Optimize we ran a preflight and got recommendations: increase batch size to 64 for short tokens, reduce kv-cache TTL for cold sessions, and enable prefix caching for our high-value agents. This reduces per-token CPU by ~25% in our sim.
[12:55] Riley Zhang: We also recommend a hybrid model routing: prioritize the larger non-quant variant for authenticated flows and use quant variants for lower-latency, low-cost paths.

[13:10] (20 minute synthetic run continues; logs streaming)
[13:40] Marcus Lee: I'm looking at the trace where fallback_variant=quant8 occurred — the response drift looked small but sometimes it changed completion style. How do we audit that?
[13:51] Alex Soto: Each fallback has a linked eval snapshot. You can diff completions in the Console's 'regression' tab and tie them to prompt-sets. We can also set an automatic rollback if drift > threshold.

[14:10] Priya Nair: We need to ensure downstream customers don't notice regressions; is there an opt-in canary?
[14:16] Jordan Kim: Yes — per-route canary percentages, A/B testing, and staged rollouts are supported. You can pin a % of traffic to the fallback variant.

--- Edge case: multiple cascading network flutters ---

[15:00] Jordan Kim: Now I'm simulating cascading flutters where groups of sessions experience staggered disconnects. This surfaces interesting queue-shedding behavior — you'll see the purge thresholds trigger.
[15:20] Emily Ruiz: In a purge, is there a way to prioritise sessions by customer tier? We need VIP sessions to stay live.
[15:27] Alex Soto: Yes — priority routing based on tokens or labels. In Dedicated you can reserve a pool for VIP traffic.
[15:40] Riley Zhang: Also note the billing implications — reserved pools are billed differently, we'll include cost examples in the pricing deck.

--- Observed anomalies and imperfect transcript notes ---

[16:10] (background crosstalk)
[16:16] Liam O'Connor: Sorry, one quick — the console shows a 'stream-shed' event, is that a permanent failure?
[16:23] Jordan Kim: No, stream-shed is our term for dropping older chunks; not permanent but it affects the client assembly. We log an event for every shed.

[17:00] (several minutes of synthetic run; telemetries shown)

[24:00] Jordan Kim: Stopping the synthetic early — here's the console snapshot; you can see fallback rate peaked at 2.3% during the biggest flutter, and recovered as autoscaling added capacity.
[24:18] Marcus Lee: That's promising. Did you run the same on a cold-start Dedicated with NVM cache?
[24:25] Jordan Kim: We did a separate run — cold-start penalty was larger but with NVM-backed cache it stayed within SLO after warm-up. We'll attach that test.

--- Customer questions and objections ---

[25:10] Priya Nair: Our legal will ask about data retention in logs, and the no-training clause. Can you point to the legal addendum?
[25:20] Riley Zhang: Yes, will send SOC2 and the legal addendum. Also our Private deployment option gives full control over telemetry.
[25:30] Liam O'Connor: About latency SLOs — can we get a contractual 99th percentile?
[25:36] Riley Zhang: For Dedicated yes we can guarantee p99 with an SLA. For Hosted it's best-effort; we provide SLOs too but enterprise SLA comes with Dedicated/Reserved.

[26:00] Emily Ruiz: On the topic of timeouts, if a client reconnects after the grace window we sometimes saw 'stitching' errors. Is there tooling to reconcile partial responses?
[26:14] Alex Soto: We provide a reconciliation API that ingests the last seen message_id and attempts to replay from cached checkpoints; if checkpoint missing we provide a recovery strategy that uses embeddings to reconstruct context.

--- Recap and next steps ---

[27:00] Riley Zhang: Quick recap: we've shown the API and Console controls for kv-cache, grace windows, fallback variants, and Optimize suggestions. We ran a synthetic that stressed streaming under jitter and observed fallback behavior; agreed to share artifacts and run a pilot.
[27:20] Priya Nair: Actionables — we'll share sample session traces and provide a shortlist of priority routes.
[27:28] Riley Zhang: Great. Next steps listed in the follow-up — I'll send the benchmark template and the recording.
[27:40] Jordan Kim: I'll provision a Dedicated test pool and run the 40k-50k TPS synthetic with the NVM-backed config, attach logs.
[27:50] Marcus Lee: Sounds good. Also please add a cost estimate for 50k sustained vs 50k burst.

[28:00] (closing)
[28:05] Riley Zhang: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the deck, compliance pack, and the ops playbook link.
[28:12] Priya Nair: Thanks, that was helpful.
[28:15] (meeting ends)
